clinicalPearls: A painful subacute thyroiditis, typically following a viral upper respiratory infection
Presents with a tender, firm goitre, neck pain often radiating to the jaw or ears, and systemic upset
It follows a triphasic course of thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery
Inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) are characteristically markedly raised, unlike in other thyroiditides
Radioactive iodine uptake is low during the thyrotoxic phase because the process is destructive
It is managed with analgesia or anti-inflammatory drugs, or corticosteroids for severe pain; beta-blockade eases thyrotoxic symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: De Quervain thyroiditis is a self-limiting inflammatory thyroiditis widely attributed to a viral or post-viral immune response, with a granulomatous infiltrate damaging thyroid follicles. Follicular destruction releases stored hormone, producing a transient thyrotoxic phase, after which hormone depletion causes a hypothyroid phase before the gland recovers. The intense inflammation accounts for the pain, tenderness and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and the destructive (rather than hyperfunctioning) mechanism explains the low radioiodine uptake. Although virally triggered, it is not a suppurative infection of the gland.
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests through the phases
Radioactive iodine uptake (low in the thyrotoxic phase)
Follow-up thyroid function to detect persistent hypothyroidism
redFlags: Features suggesting suppurative thyroiditis (high fever, fluctuant tender mass)
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover normal thyroid function within months, though a minority develop permanent hypothyroidism, and recurrence is uncommon.
pitfalls: Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs, which are ineffective in destructive thyroiditis
Confusing it with suppurative thyroiditis or Graves disease
Overlooking the markedly raised inflammatory markers as a diagnostic clue
Not following up for permanent hypothyroidism
management: Relieve pain with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, escalating to systemic corticosteroids for severe or unremitting pain
Control thyrotoxic symptoms during the initial phase with beta-blockade
Avoid antithyroid drugs and radioiodine, as the thyrotoxicosis is destructive rather than from hormone overproduction
Support the patient through the hypothyroid phase with levothyroxine if symptomatic, usually only temporarily
Monitor thyroid function through the triphasic course and at follow-up to detect persistent hypothyroidism
Reassure that most patients recover normal thyroid function and that recurrence is uncommon
